claims.text: Controlled pre-oxidation of a TiB2 coating can form an ultra-thin, adherent alumina scale.
The engineered alumina scale will significantly improve molten-aluminum corrosion resistance relative to untreated TiB2.
Pre-oxidation or anodization at 600–700°C for 1–2 hours in a regulated oxygen atmosphere will produce the intended protective scale.
Surface texturing or an adhesion promoter can secure strong bonding of the alumina scale.
Controlled oxygen partial pressure at 600–700°C for 1–2 hours forms a dense, nanometer-scale alumina film on the TiB2 coating.
The treatment should remain effective during molten-aluminum exposure at approximately 670°C.
The treatment creates a continuous, dense, nanometer-scale alumina layer on the TiB2 surface.
The alumina layer provides a robust diffusion barrier against molten aluminum.
The pre-formed alumina scale is inert and chemically stable under the proposed exposure conditions.
The alumina scale inhibits penetration by molten aluminum and reactive species.
Inhibiting penetration reduces interfacial reactions and corrosion of the underlying TiB2.
Treated samples will exhibit a lower corrosion rate, less interfacial degradation, and greater longevity than untreated TiB2 coatings.
Untreated TiB2 coatings traditionally corrode faster and degrade more severely during molten-aluminum exposure.
Extreme thermal cycling or mechanical stresses beyond the alumina layer's adhesion limit may compromise protection.
Long-term adhesion and durability of the alumina scale under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading are uncertain.
A controlled comparison will expose treated and untreated TiB2-coated samples to molten aluminum at approximately 670°C for multiple durations under otherwise identical conditions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant corrosion-rate reduction together with failure to retain a continuous, adherent alumina layer would falsify the hypothesis.
